passage: So, I'm Akash. Dhruv and I had been married three years, and everyone kept asking when we'd have a baby. My mother, his aunts, even the neighbour. I realised we'd never actually talked about it properly. So one weekend we took a notebook to the park. Big questions: are we ready financially? Who takes leave? How do we want to discipline a child, without hitting like our parents did? We didn't agree on everything. Dhruv assumed I'd take all the leave. I didn't. That was a tense afternoon. But we worked out that he'd take time off too, and that we'd save for a year first. We aren't in a hurry now. It feels like our decision, not everyone else's.

qa.q: Where did Akash and Dhruv take their notebook?
qa.a: They took it to the park.

qa.q: Why was that afternoon tense for Akash?
qa.a: Dhruv assumed Akash would take all the leave, and Akash disagreed, which exposed an unspoken expectation.

qa.q: What made their conversation a good step toward parenthood?
qa.a: They discussed money, leave and parenting values openly, and agreed on shared care and a savings plan.

qa.q: How might their families see the couple's decision to wait a year?
qa.a: The relatives who kept asking may feel impatient, but the couple now has clear reasons of their own.

grounding: Shows a couple reflecting on readiness, finances, parenting values and sharing care before having a child.

passage: I'm Arnab, Pooja's colleague and friend. Pooja and her husband were thinking about having a baby. At lunch she'd bring printouts: childcare costs, leave policies from both their companies. At first I teased her about making a spreadsheet for a baby. She didn't laugh. She said she'd seen her mother give up work and never get it back, and she wanted to decide on purpose. One day she was upset because her husband's company offered almost no paternity leave. She seemed worried he wouldn't be involved. A few weeks later she said they'd agreed he'd use his holiday days and she'd return part-time. I don't know how they'll manage in the end. But I stopped teasing her.

qa.q: What did Pooja bring to lunch?
qa.a: She brought printouts of childcare costs and leave policies.

qa.q: Why did Pooja want to decide about parenthood so carefully?
qa.a: She had seen her mother give up work and never get it back, and she feared the same thing happening to her.

qa.q: How could a friend like Arnab better support Pooja?
qa.a: By listening and taking her planning seriously instead of teasing her about it.

qa.q: Why did Arnab stop teasing Pooja?
qa.a: Arnab came to understand how important and real her concerns were after she explained them.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young woman carefully weigh readiness, money and shared care before parenthood.

passage:
Day one: Mahima's sister arrived with her six-month-old for a weekend. Darshan held the baby for five minutes and handed her back when she cried. "We're definitely ready," he joked. Mahima wasn't laughing.

Day two: The baby woke four times. Mahima noticed she did every waking while Darshan slept. She said nothing, but made a note.

Two weeks later: At dinner Mahima brought it up. "If we have a child, will you get up at night too?" Darshan was quiet, then admitted he'd assumed she'd do more. "I don't want that," he said slowly. "I just never thought about it." They agreed to learn more first, from friends with babies, before deciding anything.

qa.q: How many times did the baby wake on day two?
qa.a: The baby woke four times.

qa.q: Why wasn't Mahima laughing at Darshan's joke?
qa.a: She sensed he wasn't taking the reality of caring for a baby seriously, which worried her.

qa.q: What step did the couple agree on before deciding?
qa.a: To learn more from friends with babies before making any decision about children.

qa.q: How might Darshan's view change after the conversation?
qa.a: He realised he'd assumed Mahima would do more, and he started thinking seriously about sharing care.

grounding: Shows a couple, over a few weeks, reflecting on readiness and equal sharing of care before parenthood.

passage: Zeenat, you ask how I knew I was ready for a baby. Your Tanuja Maasi will be honest: I didn't, fully. Nobody does. But at twenty-four, before we tried, your uncle and I did something my friends found strange: we sat down with a notebook for a month of Sundays. Money first: could we manage if I took a year off? Barely, so we dropped the plan for a second scooter. Then values. He wanted strict discipline, the way he was raised. I didn't. We argued, then agreed: no hitting, ever, and we talk before any punishment. Then the practical part: who wakes at night, who stays home when the child is sick. He said, 'Half and half.' I made him write it down. When Riya came, he did the night feeds on alternate days, and yes, I showed him the notebook when he forgot. Readiness is not a feeling, beta. It's conversations.

qa.q: Which plan did Tanuja and her husband drop to manage money?
qa.a: The plan to buy a second scooter.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel about her readiness before trying for a baby?
qa.a: Unsure; she admits she did not fully know, which is why she wanted to talk everything through first.

qa.q: What topics did Tanuja and her husband cover, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Money, parenting values like no hitting, and sharing night and sick-day care, so they began parenthood with agreements instead of assumptions.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's husband have felt when she showed him the notebook?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit sheepish, but reminded of his own promise, which kept the care shared.

grounding: An aunt recalls preparing for parenthood by talking through money, values and equal sharing of care.

passage: Hansa was four months pregnant when Santosh's factory in Rajkot switched him to rotating night shifts. Their savings were thin, and her mother lived three hundred kilometres away. One Sunday, over dal-bhaat, Hansa said, 'I don't want to be the only one who knows how to bathe the baby.' Santosh went quiet, then admitted he was scared he wouldn't know how. They made a plan on the back of a calendar. He would ask his supervisor for day shifts for the first two months, even at lower pay. He would join her antenatal classes at the government hospital on his days off. They would manage the budget by skipping the new TV. And they talked about what kind of parents they wanted to be: less shouting than they had grown up with. The supervisor gave him six weeks of day shifts, not eight. Not perfect. Santosh circled the date anyway.

qa.q: Where did Santosh plan to attend classes with Hansa?
qa.a: Antenatal classes at the government hospital, on his days off.

qa.q: Why did Santosh go quiet when Hansa spoke about bathing the baby?
qa.a: He was scared he would not know how to care for the baby, which he then admitted.

qa.q: How did they prepare despite thin savings and night shifts?
qa.a: By asking for day shifts, attending classes together, skipping a purchase to manage money, and agreeing on the kind of parents they wanted to be.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh admitted his fear?
qa.a: Relieved that he was honest and willing to learn, which made sharing the care feel possible.

grounding: Shows an expecting couple preparing for parenthood under shift-work and money constraints while planning to share care.
